title: Operation Mincemeat: How A Corpse Fooled the Nazis
summary: Josh and Chuck cover Operation Mincemeat, the World War Two British deception plan that used the corpse of Welsh drifter Glyndwr Michael, dressed as fictitious Royal Marine "Major William Martin," to convince the Nazis that the Allies would invade Greece and Sardinia rather than Sicily in 1943. The episode traces the origins in Ian Fleming's Trout Memo and the Basil Thompson idea, the XX Committee led by Montagu and Chumley, the fabricated backstory including a fiancée named Pam, the body's acquisition from Sir Bentley Purchase at St. Pancras mortuary, the planted letter with the sardine joke, the submarine drop off Huelva, Spain, the Spanish handling of the body, German agent Carlo Clausen's role, and Enigma/Bletchley Park intelligence confirming the deception. Hitler moved a Panzer division to Greece, and the Allied invasion of Sicily (Operation Husky) cost far fewer lives than expected. The episode closes with book recommendations and a listener mail segment about bread crusts.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about baldness and hats, then introduce Operation Mincemeat as one of the most successful military deception plans in history, comparing it to Operation Fortitude and the Ghost Army.

segments.title: Allied strategy and the Sicily target
segments.summary: The hosts describe the stalemate in Europe under Hitler's Fortress Europe, Churchill's proposed attack on Europe's underbelly, and the Casablanca Conference that set the July invasion of Sicily as Operation Husky.

segments.title: The Trout Memo and the corpse idea
segments.summary: Admiral John Godfrey's assistant Ian Fleming wrote the Trout Memo in 1939 with fifty-one deception suggestions, including a corpse dressed as an airman with fake documents, an idea borrowed from Basil Thompson's novel. Churchill liked the idea, and the XX Committee was led by Montagu and Charles Chumley.

segments.title: Building the fake persona of Major William Martin
segments.summary: The planners chose Spain as the place to deliver the fake courier to a gullible Nazi agent. They built the fictitious Major William Martin with pocket litter, a fiancée named Pam whose photo came from a secretary, and love letters written by Hester Leggett. Montagu and the secretary had a real affair.

segments.title: Finding the body
segments.summary: The team needed a military-age body that died of pneumonia so an autopsy would appear to show drowning. Sir Bentley Purchase at St. Pancras mortuary supplied Glyndwr Michael, a Welsh drifter who had died of rat poison. A lookalike officer was used for the photograph.

segments.title: The planted letter and submarine drop
segments.summary: The key document was a letter hinting that the invasion would come through Greece and Sardinia, with Sicily as cover, including a sardine joke and a hidden eyelash to detect tampering. A submarine carried the body in a cylinder off Spain and released it toward Huelva, where it was found by a fisherman.

segments.title: Spanish handling, German agents and the Enigma result
segments.summary: British diplomats sought the briefcase, the Spanish refused to autopsy the Catholic body, and German agent Carlo Clausen took the letter to Berlin. Bletchley Park's Enigma intelligence confirmed the Germans had swallowed the deception. Hitler moved a Panzer division to Greece, and the Allied invasion of Sicily cost far fewer lives than expected.

segments.title: Aftermath, sources and listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts note Glyndwr Michael's posthumous military honors in Spain, recommend books on Operation Mincemeat, and read a listener email about the lucky bread crust.

segments.title: Listener mail: bread crust
segments.summary: A listener named Ted describes calling bread crust pieces the lucky piece for his daughters, and says children under eleven will fight for it.
